note: Interpretive content for the Big Five analysis. Levels come from the bands in bigfive_mapping.json: low = first band, mid = second, high = third. Combinations fire when every listed dimension is at the listed level.

sources.base_text: Rewritten from the English domain texts in b5-result-text (MIT, github.com/Alheimsins/b5-result-text), which reproduce John A. Johnson's IPIP-NEO narrative report. Not copied: every sentence here is reworded, softened, and put in the second person.
sources.inspiration: Daniel Nettle, Personality: What Makes You the Way You Are (Oxford, 2007). Read in full; see src/lib/knowledge/nettle.json. The costs-and-benefits framing, and the 'about' text below, are drawn from Nettle's own framing of each trait, cited by chapter and page.
sources.status: Nettle content now verified against the book. Big Five base text is still from b5-result-text/Johnson's IPIP-NEO report (see base_text above), not from Nettle - the two are blended: Johnson for the low/mid/high descriptions, Nettle for the 'about' framing and the trait combinations.

high.strength: You bring energy into a room and find it easy to connect, start things and rally people.
high.watch: Constant input can crowd out reflection; some quiet time helps you hear yourself.

mid.note: You move between company and solitude as the situation asks, without a strong pull either way.

low.strength: You listen well, think before you speak and are comfortable in your own company.
low.watch: Staying in the background can mean your ideas go unheard; choose a few moments to speak first.

EXT.about: Extraversion is about how responsive your brain's positive-emotion system is: desire, excitement and joy that activate when you pursue something you value, whether that's status, new relationships, mastery or plain resources (Nettle, ch.3). Sociability is a visible symptom of this, not the core of the trait. Being reserved isn't shyness: that's better predicted by Neuroticism, not low Extraversion. A low scorer isn't afraid of people, just gets less reward from company and needs less of it. Extraversion predicts how much you socialise and how fast you make contacts, but not how well those relationships go - that's Agreeableness. A highly extraverted, less agreeable person can enjoy friction rather than avoid it. Nettle names the trade-off plainly: the benefit is pursuing and capturing more of what you want; the cost, at the higher end, is physical risk and instability in close relationships (ch.7, Table 4).

high.strength: People feel cared for around you; you smooth tension and notice who is left out.
high.watch: Putting others first can turn into saying yes when you mean no.

mid.note: You are warm with people you trust and more guarded with those you don't yet know.

low.strength: You say what you think and hold your ground, which is valuable when honesty matters.
low.watch: Directness can land harder than you intend; a word of warmth first often helps it be heard.

AGR.about: Agreeableness comes down to 'other-regarding preferences' - caring about someone else's outcome, not only your own (Nettle, ch.6). It rests on theory of mind: mentalizing (working out what someone else believes or wants) and empathizing (feeling it with them). Higher scorers are considerate, generous and trusting, and are usually well liked; people who mentalize well tend to have larger, smoother social networks. Lower scorers put their own judgement first and are more sceptical of others' motives, which is genuinely useful where a tough, objective call is needed. Neither end is better; they suit different situations. Nettle's summary: the benefit is harmonious relationships; the cost, at the higher end, is not putting yourself first, which can mean losing out on status (ch.7, Table 4).

high.strength: You are reliable, organised and finish what you start.
high.watch: High standards can become rigidity or self-criticism when things don't go to plan.

mid.note: You bring structure where it matters and stay relaxed about the rest.

low.strength: You are flexible and spontaneous, and adapt quickly when plans change.
low.watch: Important but dull tasks can slip; a small routine for the essentials frees you for the rest.

CON.about: Conscientiousness is about being able to give up a bigger reward right now for a better outcome later (Nettle, ch.5, drawing on the Iowa Gambling Task). Higher scorers set goals and pursue them persistently, which brings reliability and achievement, though it can tip into perfectionism or overwork. Lower scorers are drawn more strongly to the immediate payoff, which makes them flexible and spontaneous but can let long-term plans slip. Nettle notes that struggling to resist immediate reward is shared by people with gambling and substance-use difficulties - worth naming as a real vulnerability, not a character flaw, when it shows up strongly. Nettle's summary: the benefit is planning and self-control; the cost, at the higher end, is rigidity and a loss of spontaneity (ch.7, Table 4).

high.strength: You feel things deeply, which makes you perceptive about moods and risks.
high.watch: Stress hits quickly and can linger; regular regulation practices (breath, movement, sleep) make a real difference.

mid.note: You feel stress clearly but usually recover with some time or space.

low.strength: You stay even under pressure and recover quickly from setbacks.
low.watch: Calm can hide real problems from you or from others; check in on what you actually feel.

NEU.about: Emotional reactivity (what research calls neuroticism) is the mirror of Extraversion: how responsive your negative-emotion system is - fear, anxiety, shame, guilt, disgust, sadness (Nettle, ch.4). These emotions evolved to make you detect and avoid what was dangerous. Nettle applies the 'smoke detector principle' here: it's evolutionarily safer for a warning system to sound too often than to miss a real threat once. High reactivity is that detector set sensitively - it costs you frequent false alarms, but the alternative used to cost far more. This trait responds well to practice: breathwork, movement, sleep and reflection all lower reactivity over time. Nettle's own summary names the trade-off: the benefit is vigilance and striving; the cost, at the higher end, is anxiety and depression (ch.7, Table 4).

high.strength: You are curious and imaginative, and enjoy new ideas, art and abstract thinking.
high.watch: Chasing the next idea can leave earlier ones unfinished.

mid.note: You are open to new ideas when they connect to what already matters to you.

low.strength: You are practical and grounded, and trust what has been tested.
low.watch: Unfamiliar approaches may get dismissed before they've had a fair look.

OPN.about: Openness correlates with IQ (Nettle cites roughly r=0.3, stronger for verbal than spatial intelligence) but is its own trait, not intelligence under another name (ch.7). It's a broad pull toward engaging with complex ideas, art and experience across the board, not a preference for one activity over another. Nettle takes the poet or artist as the clearest real-world example: metaphorical thinking, a readiness to challenge convention, and often a pull toward spiritual or unusual experience. Lower scorers prefer the concrete and proven, which is its own kind of strength: less prone to chasing every new idea, more grounded in what's tested. Nettle's summary: the benefit is artistic sensibility; the cost, at the higher end, is unusual beliefs and, rarely, a higher likelihood of psychosis-spectrum conditions - one reason very high Openness deserves the same non-judgemental read as any other trait, not more (ch.7, Table 4).

combinations.text: Driven and conscientious, with a strong inner critic: high standards can turn into worry about falling short. Progress you can see (lists, small wins) quiets the critic.
Steady and reliable under pressure. Others likely lean on you when things get busy, so watch that you don't carry everyone's load.
Warm and sociable: people tend to feel welcome around you, and you are often the one who brings a group together.
You tend to process stress inwardly. Quiet time helps, and so does telling one trusted person what's going on before it builds up.
Expressive and responsive: your moods show quickly and ripple through your social world. Naming the feeling out loud often helps it pass.
Full of ideas, less drawn to the routine of finishing them. A simple structure for follow-through multiplies what you create.
You combine imagination with follow-through, a mix that suits building new things from idea to finished work.
Direct and demanding, of yourself and of others. Effective, though your edge may land harder than you mean it to.
Very attuned to others' feelings, and inclined to take them on as your own. Clear boundaries protect that sensitivity.

nature_and_change: Twin and adoption studies put each trait's heritable component at roughly 50% (Nettle, ch.8, p.210-211). The rest isn't explained by upbringing either: shared family environment - the same parents, same household - has close to no measurable effect on adult personality once you compare identical twins raised together with identical twins raised apart, or adopted siblings with their biological ones. What shapes the other half is individual experience: things that happened to you and not to a sibling, which research still understands poorly (ch.8, p.213-216). Practically: there's no right or wrong level of any trait here, only a level that fits some situations better than others (ch.3, p.102-103). And your score today is not a life sentence from your childhood - your baseline and any retakes will show your own direction.
